ex:benzene-symmetric-projector:
Example Benzene as the assembly projector e_{(2,2,2),(6)}. Benzene is the special case \lambda = (2,2,2) of the assembly projector: three acetylene sub-units, each contributing two carbons, give six carbon strands. The projector e_{(2,2,2),(6)} projects the six \pi-electrons onto the symmetric Wedderburn block \mu = (6).

Projection onto \mu = (6) is the categorical content of aromaticity. The shared \pi-content is spread symmetrically over all six carbons. The partition \lambda = (2,2,2) is forced by the assembly of three two-carbon units. The symmetric block is selected by the binding LP only when the geometry supports delocalisation.
rem:aromaticity-as-symmetric-projection:
Remark Aromaticity, stability, and why breaking a ring releases a lot. Stability requires three steps:

  1. Existence. For any \lambda the symmetric-block projector e_{\lambda,(N)} exists.
  2. Optimality. Among admissible configurations, the binding LP/SDP selects the one minimising the trace objective under Frobenius positivity. Stability is this selection.
  3. Energetics. The binding energy is the trace-weight gap between the selected block and the next configuration. For the six-carbon ring, the threaded T(2,6) configuration carries Alexander weight \approx 3 while the open chain carries weight 5. The gap 5 - 3 = 2, scaled by the molecular energy unit, is the ring-closure resonance energy.

The ring's projector e_{(2,2,2),(6)} is irreducible over all six strands. One cannot open the ring a single bond at a time. Breaking it collapses the entire symmetric block back to the localised chain, paying the whole weight-gap cooperatively. This irreducibility of the global projector is the categorical content of aromatic stability.
sec:electron-shells-intro:
Before molecules are assembled, atomic bonding capacity is determined. The electron shell translates atomic shell structure into the number of trefoils its braid admits. The aufbau principle is recovered by minimising the dual cost \Phi_1. This yields the standard valence electron count and the octet rule.

Two refinements sharpen this model. First, the normal-form term count in the quotient atom combinatorially detects closed shells. Second, the palindromicity of the normal-form histogram characterises s, p, d, f orbital types. Take these shell capacities as given and apply the construction to H_2, CO, CO_2, CH_4, and C_6H_6.
def:electron-shell-braid-capacity: Definition Electron shell as braid bonding capacity. In the atomic braid \mathcal{A}(Z, N), each of the Z electrons is the word \sigma_0\sigma_1\sigma_0 in H_3(q) (closure: the Hopf link), Hopf-linked to the nuclear core. A bonding site is a position in the atomic braid available to an electron. The shell capacity is the number of bonding sites at each shell level, determined by the electron arrangement that minimises \Phi_1.
rem:electron-shell-braid-capacity-remark: Remark Shell filling order. An atom with Z electrons fills shells in order of increasing \Phi_1 contribution.
def:atomic-valence-open-sites:
Definition Valence and lone pairs as open bonding sites. Let Z_{\mathrm{val}} be the number of valence electrons of an atom of atomic number Z and n_{\mathrm{val}} its outermost shell level. The valence of the atom, the number of open bonding sites available for covalent bonds, is

  v(Z) = \min\bigl(Z_{\mathrm{val}},\; 2n_{\mathrm{val}}^2 - Z_{\mathrm{val}}\bigr).

A lone pair is an electron pair whose \Phi_1 contribution is lower when bound to a single nucleus than when shared.

prop:shell-capacity-self-square:
Proposition Shell capacity 2n^2 as the self-square of the angular q-dimension. For every principal shell level n \in \mathbb{N}, the number of orbital sub-states is the sum of the sub-shell multiplicities 2\ell+1 over \ell = 0,\ldots,n-1,

  \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1} (2\ell+1) \;=\; n^2,

and the electron capacity of the shell, carrying the spin factor 2, is

  \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1} 2(2\ell+1) \;=\; 2n^2 .

Both are the q\to 1 value of the bar-even self-square [n]_q^2.

This is the self-fusion of a single angular q-dimension, not a product of two independent symmetries. The angular q-dimension is the bar-even (cosh) Chebyshev evaluation [n]_q = U_{n-1}\!\bigl((q+q^{-1})/2\bigr) of the shell element. The q-Clebsch–Gordan rule decomposes its self-square into the sub-shell multiplicities,

  [n]_q^2 \;=\; \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1} [2\ell+1]_q
  \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
  2[n]_q^2\big|_{q=1} \;=\; 2n^2 ,

since [2\ell+1]_q\big|_{q=1} = 2\ell+1. The \mathrm{SO}(4)=\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{SU}(2) "(j,j) doubling" of the hydrogenic shell is here the self-square V\otimes V of one object. The second factor is a copy of the first, tied by the coproduct. No second compact \mathrm{SU}(2) is required. The compact (\cos/\sin, root of unity) and non-compact (\cosh/\sinh, real q) forms are the two real forms of one \mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C}).

The q=1 integer identities above are proved (sum of the first n odd numbers, by induction). The residual modeling assumption — that the electron shell space is this self-square, rather than the count merely agreeing with it — is recorded as structural input.

Shell n n^2 Capacity 2n^2 Sub-shells [2\ell+1]_{q=1}
1 1 2 1
2 4 8 1 + 3
3 9 18 1 + 3 + 5
4 16 32 1 + 3 + 5 + 7
conj:shell-space-is-self-square:
Conjecture The shell state space is the self-square of the angular object. Write V_j for the \mathrm{SU}(2)_q irrep of spin j, of q-dimension [2j+1]_q, and let j_n = (n-1)/2 be the spin of the angular object of principal shell n, so that \dim_q V_{j_n} = [n]_q. Then the orbital state space of shell n is the self-fusion of that one object with itself,

  \mathcal{O}_n \;\cong\; V_{j_n} \otimes V_{j_n} ,

the second tensor factor being a copy of the first, tied to it by the coproduct. In particular \dim_q \mathcal{O}_n = [n]_q^2.

The spin labelling is the one used in The orbital space at shell n is the space of framing-k sections of the normal bundle: V_\ell there is the sub-shell irrep of dimension 2\ell+1, which is V_j here at integer j = \ell.

This is the one step of the 2n^2 shell-capacity account that is not derived. Everything downstream of it is exact.

What the conjecture is not. It is not a claim that a second symmetry group acts. The (j,j) doubling that the hydrogenic shell classically receives from \mathrm{SO}(4) = \mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{SU}(2) and its Runge–Lenz vector is here internal to a single object. The compact (\cos/\sin, root of unity) and non-compact (\cosh/\sinh, real q) pictures are the two real forms of one \mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C}), so no second compact \mathrm{SU}(2) is required or postulated.

What follows exactly. Given the identification, the q-Clebsch–Gordan rule decomposes the self-square into the sub-shells,

  V_{j_n} \otimes V_{j_n} \;\cong\; \bigoplus_{\ell=0}^{n-1} V_\ell ,
  \qquad\text{hence}\qquad
  [n]_q^2 \;=\; \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1} [2\ell+1]_q ,

which is Shell capacity 2n^2 as the self-square of the angular q-dimension and, at q = 1, the periodic-table capacities 2n^2 = 2,8,18,32,\ldots. Clearing the common denominator (q - q^{-1}) turns this into a polynomial identity over \mathbb{Z}[q,q^{-1}], proved for every n.

Falsifiable content. The conjecture asserts more than a coincidence of counts. It fixes the sub-shell multiplicities as the q-integers [2\ell+1]_q, and not only their q \to 1 values 2\ell+1; a resolved sub-shell structure departing from [2\ell+1]_q at q \neq 1 would refute it. The sub-shell decomposition is derived from the conjectural hypothesis rather than assumed alongside it, and a concrete counterexample shows that the hypothesis is not satisfied by an arbitrary dimension function.

Relation to the normal-bundle model. The orbital space at shell n is the space of framing-k sections of the normal bundle describes the same space \mathcal{O}_n geometrically, as framing-k sections of the trefoil's normal bundle in Bring's surface cut off by a q-Laplacian eigenvalue bound. The two are independent descriptions of one object: the present conjecture supplies its categorical structure, the normal-bundle conjecture its geometric realisation. Establishing an isomorphism between them would close both at once.
rem:electron-shell-2n2-capacity:
Remark The 2n^2 capacity needs no second compact \mathrm{SU}(2). The shell capacity 2n^2 was for a period recorded here as an open problem requiring an \mathrm{SO}(4)-type accidental degeneracy to bundle the angular-momentum levels \ell = 0,\ldots,n-1 into a single principal shell. That framing is withdrawn. The count is obtained in Shell capacity 2n^2 as the self-square of the angular q-dimension from the self-fusion of one angular object, and the mechanism it attributed the count to is not the one at work.

The classical route to 2n^2 runs through the Runge–Lenz vector: the hydrogenic bound-state symmetry enlarges from \mathrm{SO}(3) to \mathrm{SO}(4) = \mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{SU}(2), and the shell is the (j,j) representation of dimension (2j+1)^2 = n^2. The doubling is a product of two commuting factors, and asking which second compact \mathrm{SU}(2) supplies the second factor is the natural question in that setting.

In the present framework the doubling is not a product of two symmetries. The shell-n object is one Chebyshev element U_{n-1}, whose bar-even evaluation at (q + q^{-1})/2 is the angular q-dimension [n]_q and whose bar-odd evaluation at (q - q^{-1})/2 is the radial tower. Its self-fusion V \otimes V supplies the second factor as a copy of the first, tied by the coproduct, and q-Clebsch–Gordan then returns the sub-shells:

  [n]_q^2 \;=\; \sum_{\ell=0}^{n-1} [2\ell+1]_q ,
  \qquad
  2[n]_q^2\big|_{q=1} \;=\; 2n^2 .

The compact (\cos/\sin, root of unity) and non-compact (\cosh/\sinh, real q) forms are the two real forms of one \mathfrak{sl}(2,\mathbb{C}), unified by the complex volume. No second compact \mathrm{SU}(2) is required, and none is postulated.

What survives as open is narrower, and is stated separately as The shell state space is the self-square of the angular object: that the shell state space is the self-square, rather than carrying a dimension that happens to agree with it. The remaining shell-structure gap, the ordering of subshells beyond the capacity count, is a separate matter and is not addressed by either block.
prop:shell-filling-rule:
Proposition Shell filling minimises \Phi_1 (aufbau from LP dual). The ground-state electron configuration of atom (Z, N) is the assignment of Z electron trefoils to bonding sites that minimises the total \Phi_1 of the atomic braid, reproducing the aufbau principle. The LP dual of the electron assignment problem is:

  \max_{y} \; Z \cdot y_0
  \quad\text{s.t.}\quad
  y_0 + \sum_{n} G_{n,s} \, y_{n,s} \leq \Phi_1^{(s)}
  \;\;\forall\, \text{sites } s

where \Phi_1^{(s)} is the \Phi_1 contribution of placing an electron at site s, and G_{n,s} encodes the Gram-matrix penalty for electron-electron repulsion at shell n.
rem:shell-filling-rule-aufbau-hund:
Remark Aufbau and Hund rules from the \Phi_1 minimisation. The \Phi_1-minimisation of Shell filling minimises \Phi_1 (aufbau from LP dual) reproduces the aufbau and Hund rules:

  1. Inner shells (n < n_{\mathrm{val}}) fill completely because each additional electron in a partly filled inner shell reduces \Phi_1 more than any valence electron.

  2. Within the valence shell, electrons distribute to maximise the number of singly occupied sites (Hund's rule). Parallel electron trefoils have lower \Phi_1 than antiparallel pairs, and the ee crossing (\sigma, repulsive) is minimised when electrons occupy distinct spatial sites.

rem:shell-filling-electronegativity-ilp:
Remark Electronegativity, Parr–Pearson shadow-price hardness, and ILP generator alternation. Let E(N) denote the optimal ground-state energy of a frozen nuclear core (Z, N_{\mathrm{nuc}}) dressed by N \ge 1 bound electrons in Layer \mathcal{L}_3, with vertical ionization potential I(N) := E(N-1) - E(N) and electron affinity A_{\mathrm{ea}}(N) := E(N) - E(N+1). Because the electron count N \in \mathbb{N} is discrete, the LP dual variable y_0 governing marginal electron attachment splits at each integer N into right and left discrete shadow slopes

  \mu_+(N) := E(N+1) - E(N) = -A_{\mathrm{ea}}(N),
  \qquad
  \mu_-(N) := E(N) - E(N-1) = -I(N).

Their negative midpoint recovers Mulliken absolute electronegativity \chi_{\mathrm{M}}(N) [mulliken1934], while their jump across N recovers the Parr–Pearson chemical hardness discontinuity \eta_{\mathrm{PP}}(N) [perdew-parr-levy-balduz1982, parr-pearson1983]:

  2\,\chi_{\mathrm{M}}(N) = -\bigl(\mu_+(N) + \mu_-(N)\bigr) = I(N) + A_{\mathrm{ea}}(N),
  \qquad
  \eta_{\mathrm{PP}}(N) := I(N) - A_{\mathrm{ea}}(N) = \mu_+(N) - \mu_-(N) = E(N-1) + E(N+1) - 2E(N).

(Parr and Pearson [parr-pearson1983] also write \frac{1}{2}(I - A_{\mathrm{ea}}), differing by a conventional factor of 2.) Consequently, \eta_{\mathrm{PP}}(N) \ge 0 holds if and only if the piecewise-linear Perdew–Parr–Levy–Balduz ground-state envelope satisfies discrete convexity 2E(N) \le E(N-1) + E(N+1) [perdew-parr-levy-balduz1982]. Strict convexity \eta_{\mathrm{PP}}(N) > 0 makes charge disproportionation 2X(N) \to X(N-1) + X(N+1) strictly endothermic, with maximal shadow-slope kinks at the cumulative 2n^2 Madelung period closures

  Z_{\mathrm{noble}} \in \{2,\,10,\,18,\,36,\,54,\,86\}
  \qquad (\mathrm{He},\,\mathrm{Ne},\,\mathrm{Ar},\,\mathrm{Kr},\,\mathrm{Xe},\,\mathrm{Rn}),

generated by period capacities 2\lceil (p+2)/2\rceil^2 \in (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32).

ILP electron attachment and Hund generator alternation

Within an open shell, sequential integer-LP attachment selects at each step N \mapsto N+1 the crossing operator that minimizes |\mathrm{tr}_M| subject to Frobenius positivity G \cdot x \ge 0; see Table. The attachment sequence alternates generators (\sigma_0^{-1} versus \sigma_1^{-1}), realizing Hund's rule in the molecular Hecke algebra: electrons e_2 and e_6 (and e_7 in \mathrm{N} and \mathrm{O}) pair via \sigma_0^{-1} rather than \sigma_1^{-1} across the 2s and 2p subshells.
rem:valence-from-braid:
Remark Valence and bonding capacity from the atomic braid. The shell capacity directly determines how many covalent bonds each atom can form. An atom shares electrons only when the molecular \Phi_1 is lower than the sum of isolated atomic \Phi_1 values. Sharing reduces the total quantum dilogarithm volume.

For the first-row atoms:

Atom Valence v Lone pairs Typical bonds Example
H 1 0 1 single H--H, C--H
C 4 0 4 single, or 2 double, or 1 triple + 1 single CH_4, CO_2, HCN
N 3 1 3 single, or 1 double + 1 single, or 1 triple NH_3, NO, N_2
O 2 2 2 single, or 1 double H_2O, CO, CO_2

The octet rule emerges as a special case. Atoms with n_{\mathrm{val}} = 2 achieve \Phi_1 minimum when the second shell is complete (8 electrons = 2 \times 2^2). This is a consequence of the Hecke algebra dimension at shell level 2.

Carbon's versatile bonding (4 bonds in multiple geometries) arises because it sits at the half-filling point of the n = 2 shell: Z_{\mathrm{val}} = 4 = \frac{1}{2} \times 8. Half-filled shells have maximum \Phi_1 flexibility, allowing both \sigma-bond (single) and \pi-bond (double/triple) configurations.
conj:shell-closure-nf-term-count:
Conjecture Shell closure from NF term count. In the quotient atom model H_{Z+1}(q) — where the nuclear core is a single strand \mathcal{N} and each electron is a strand e_k — the growth ratio \gamma(Z) = n(Z)/n(Z-1) of the Gröbner–Shirshov normal form term count separates three regimes:

  \gamma(Z) \in
  \begin{cases}
    \{1\}         & \text{s-shell pairing (exact)} \\
    [1.2,\, 1.4]  & \text{p-shell pairing (approximate)} \\
    [3.0,\, 4.0]  & \text{sub-shell opening}
  \end{cases}

No Z falls in the gap (1.4, 3.0). This gap is the algebraic shell gap of the Hecke chain.

Setup

The quotient atom model. Given a neutral atom with Z protons, N neutrons, and Z electrons, quotient the nuclear core \mathcal{N}(Z, N) to a single formal variable. The resulting element lives in H_{Z+1}(q) with crossing types:

See Table 1.

The nucleus–electron crossing is the Z-fold composition (\sigma^{-1})^Z, not the scalar multiple Z \cdot \sigma^{-1}. In the braid picture, quotienting Z proton strands to one means the electron wraps Z times.

Closed form. The Hecke relation \sigma^2 = h\sigma + 1 reduces (\sigma^{-1})^Z = c_Z \sigma + d_Z with eigenvalues q^{-Z} (trivial) and (-q)^Z (sign):

  c_Z = \frac{q^{-Z} - (-1)^Z q^Z}{[2]_q}, \qquad
  d_Z = \frac{q^{-(Z+1)} + (-1)^Z q^{Z+1}}{[2]_q}

These are Chebyshev U-type polynomials in h = q - q^{-1} with the Hecke eigenvalues q^{-1} and -q as roots. The sign of c_Z alternates. It is positive for odd Z and negative for even Z. This alternation drives the pairing mechanism.

Proved (algebraic engine). The reduction (\sigma^{-1})^Z = c_Z\sigma + d_Z with these closed forms, and the sign-alternation c_Z<0 (even Z) / c_Z>0 (odd Z) with |c_Z| strictly increasing for q>1, is established rigorously by diagonalising \sigma in the two-dimensional H_2(q) (eigenvalues q,-q^{-1}, so (\sigma^{-1})^Z has eigenvalues q^{-Z},(-1)^Zq^Z). This is confirmed numerically as an exact q-independent identity to 10^{-40}. The conjectural content is how its sign-alternation propagates through the full Gröbner–Shirshov reduction of the quotient atom in H_{Z+1}(q) to the three \gamma-regimes above.

The NF. The atom is built by sequential Hopf-linking. Start with \mathcal{N} and add e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_Z one at a time, reducing via Gröbner–Shirshov at each step.

Computational evidence

The quotient NF term count for Z = 1 through 8 (corrected (\sigma^{-1})^Z crossing):

See Table 2.

The algebraic shell gap. The growth ratio \gamma falls into two bands separated by the gap (1.4, 3.0):

  • Pairing band \gamma \leq 1.4: even Z, the second electron in a sub-shell pair. For s-shells (Z = 2, 4), \gamma = 1.00 exactly (no new NF words). For p-shells (Z = 6, 8), \gamma \approx 1.25–1.30 (a few new words from the growing (\sigma^{-1})^Z coefficients).

  • Opening band \gamma \geq 3.0: odd Z, a new sub-shell electron. The NF triples or quadruples as genuinely new reduced words appear in H_{Z+1}(q).

The gap separating these bands is the algebraic shell gap. This discrete structural feature of the Hecke normal form encodes the pairing principle without input from angular momentum or spin.

Pairing mechanism

The Chebyshev sign alternation of c_Z drives pairing:

  • Odd Z (sub-shell opening): c_Z > 0, d_Z < 0. The crossing element c_Z \sigma + d_Z is \sigma-heavy. The positive \sigma coefficient creates new reduced words at higher word-lengths, expanding the NF.

  • Even Z (pairing): c_Z < 0, d_Z > 0. The crossing is identity-heavy. The negative \sigma coefficient cancels against existing NF words rather than creating new ones, suppressing growth.

For s-shells, the suppression is exact (\gamma = 1) because |c_Z| is small (0.209 at Z = 2, 0.427 at Z = 4). For p-shells, |c_Z| has grown (0.664 at Z = 6, 0.930 at Z = 8) so the suppression is approximate (\gamma \approx 1.3).

Global scaling

All coefficients in the Z-electron quotient atom carry a global prefactor Z^Z:

  \text{coeff}(\mathcal{A}(Z)) \in Z^Z \cdot \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]

For carbon (Z = 6), 6^6 = 46656 appears in every term.

Scope and limitations

The \gamma < 2 criterion detects electron pairing (every even Z), not full noble-gas shell closures (Z = 2, 10, 18, 36, \ldots). The 1D Hecke chain H_{Z+1}(q) encodes radial shell structure but lacks angular momentum. It cannot distinguish 2p^2 (Z = 6) from 2p^6 (Z = 10, neon). Detecting noble-gas closures requires a product structure H_{Z+1}(q) \otimes \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SO}(3)) where the Hecke chain handles radial pairing and the rotation group handles sub-shell degeneracy 2\ell + 1.

conj:palindromicity-orbital-type:
Conjecture Palindromicity and orbital type. The word-length histogram of the quotient atom NF is palindromic (Poincaré-dual) if and only if all occupied sub-shells have angular momentum \ell = 0 (s-type). Palindromicity breaks at the first electron with \ell \geq 1 (p-type or higher).

Computational evidence

From the quotient atom model, the palindromicity status at each Z:

See Table 1.

Transition at Z = 5: the first p-electron breaks palindromicity. Through Z = 4 (pure s-shells), the histogram is perfectly symmetric.

Physical interpretation

Palindromicity of the NF histogram is Poincaré duality in the Bruhat lattice of S_{Z+1}. The word-length distribution \{n_0, n_1, \ldots, n_L\} satisfies n_k = n_{L-k}. This duality holds when the NF occupies a self-dual sub-lattice. This happens precisely when the electron chain has no angular momentum (pure s-orbitals).

The p-electron introduces a chiral crossing that breaks the left-right symmetry of the braid word. In the Hecke algebra, this corresponds to a representation that is not self-dual under the longest-element involution w \mapsto w_0 w.

Conjectured grading

The degree of palindromic defect is the minimum number of histogram entries that must be removed to restore palindromicity. This should equal 2\ell, where \ell is the angular momentum quantum number of the outermost occupied sub-shell:

See Table 2.

This provides a purely algebraic definition of orbital angular momentum: \ell is half the palindromic defect of the Hecke algebra NF histogram.

sec:h2-computation-intro: The smallest covalent molecule comes next. The hydrogen molecule H_2 as a braid in H_4(q) places two protons and two electrons on four strands and lets them share a single trefoil. The LP dual selects the optimal H_2 binding, determines the bond order, and provides the binding energy. The predicted H_2 binding energy is compared with the spectroscopic value. The covalent channel eigenvalue ratio yields the equilibrium internuclear separation. This sets the template for the heteronuclear and polyatomic cases.
def:h2-molecular-braid: Definition Hydrogen molecule H_2 as a braid in H_4(q). The hydrogen molecule H_2 is the molecular braid of two hydrogen atoms sharing one electron pair.
rem:h2-molecular-braid-remark:
Remark Staged construction of the hydrogen molecule. The construction of H_2 proceeds in three stages.

Stage 1: Build two hydrogen atoms

Each hydrogen atom is an atomic braid in H_2(q): one proton \mathfrak{p} and one electron e, with the \mathcal{B}_3-dressed \mathfrak{p}e crossing.

Atom 1: \mathcal{A}_1 = [\mathfrak{p}_1, e_1] with dressed eigenvalues (q^5, -q^{-5}).

Atom 2: \mathcal{A}_2 = [\mathfrak{p}_2, e_2] with dressed eigenvalues (q^5, -q^{-5}).

Stage 2: Embed in H_4(q) and apply inter-atomic crossings

The molecular braid lives in H_4(q) with strand ordering [\mathfrak{p}_1, e_1, \mathfrak{p}_2, e_2]. The six pairwise crossings are:

See Table.

The covalent channel is the e_1\mathfrak{p}_2 crossing (\sigma_1). Electron 1 from atom 1 is attracted to proton 2 of atom 2. By symmetry, e_2 is also attracted to \mathfrak{p}_1 via the \mathfrak{p}_1 e_2 crossing. This produces the shared-electron bond.

Stage 3: Transfer matrix chain

The four-strand transfer matrix product is:

  \hat{V}^{H_2} = T_{\mathfrak{p}_1 e_1}^{\mathrm{dressed}}
  \cdot T_{e_1 \mathfrak{p}_2}
  \cdot T_{\mathfrak{p}_2 e_2}^{\mathrm{dressed}}

where:

  T_{\mathfrak{p}e}^{\mathrm{dressed}} =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    q^{-5} + d & q^{-5} - q^5 \\
    1 & q^5 + d
  \end{pmatrix},
  \qquad
  T_{e_1\mathfrak{p}_2} =
  \begin{pmatrix}
    q^{-1} + d & q^{-1} - q \\
    1 & q + d
  \end{pmatrix}

with d = -(q - q^{-1}). At q_0 \approx 1.110:

  • T_{\mathfrak{p}e}^{\mathrm{dressed}}: eigenvalues q^5 \approx 1.680 and -q^{-5} \approx -0.595
  • T_{e_1\mathfrak{p}_2} (covalent): eigenvalues q \approx 1.110 and -q^{-1} \approx -0.901

rem:h2-covalent-channel-interference:
Remark Covalent channel eigenvalue ratio and optimal strand ordering. The covalent crossing eigenvalue ratio q/q^{-1} = q^2 \approx 1.231 is closer to 1 than the dressed atomic ratio q^5/q^{-5} = q^{10} \approx 2.826. The covalent channel has less destructive interference than the intra-atomic channels. The shared electron reduces \Phi_1 relative to two isolated atoms.

Strand orderings

The LP dual optimises over all 4! = 24 permutations of [\mathfrak{p}_1, e_1, \mathfrak{p}_2, e_2]. By the symmetry (\mathfrak{p}_1, e_1) \leftrightarrow (\mathfrak{p}_2, e_2), there are 12 distinct orderings. The optimal ordering places the two electron-proton pairs interleaved:

  [\mathfrak{p}_1, e_2, \mathfrak{p}_2, e_1]

Each electron is adjacent to the other atom's proton (the covalent partner). This maximises the number of \sigma^{-1} (attractive) crossings in adjacent positions, minimising \Phi_1.
prop:h2-lp-dual-binding:
Proposition LP dual gives optimal H_2 binding. Conditional on Seven-term atomic mass formula with q-integer coefficients. The LP dual of the H_2 molecular braid selects the interleaved ordering [\mathfrak{p}_1, e_2, \mathfrak{p}_2, e_1] as the ground state, with molecular volume:

  \Phi_1^{H_2} = \sum_{i=0}^{2} \ln\lvert \hat{V}_i^{H_2} \rvert

The primal program minimises the Markov trace of the molecular braid over all strand orderings and electron assignments:

  \min_{\pi \in S_4} \; \Phi_1\!\left(
    T_{\pi(0)\pi(1)} \cdot T_{\pi(1)\pi(2)} \cdot T_{\pi(2)\pi(3)}
  \right)

subject to:

  • Each proton appears exactly once
  • Each electron appears exactly once
  • The shared electron is Hopf-linked to both protons (covalent constraint)

The dual program maximises the shadow price of the covalent constraint:

  \max_{y} \; y_{\mathrm{cov}}
  \quad\text{s.t.}\quad
  y_{\mathrm{cov}} \leq
  \Phi_1^{\mathrm{separated}} - \Phi_1^{H_2}(\pi)
  \;\;\forall\, \pi

where \Phi_1^{\mathrm{separated}} = 2 \times \Phi_1^{H} is the \Phi_1 of two isolated hydrogen atoms.

Strong duality holds. The optimal y_{\mathrm{cov}}^* equals the binding energy per shared electron. At q_0:

Numerical evaluation

Two isolated H atoms (dressed):

  \Phi_1^{H} = \ln\lvert V^{H} \rvert
  = \ln\lvert q^5 \cdot (-(q-q^{-1})) + q^{-5} \cdot 1 \rvert

At q_0 \approx 1.110, (q-q^{-1}) \approx 0.208:

  • V^{H} = -q^5(q - q^{-1}) + q^{-5} \approx -1.680 \times 0.208 + 0.595 \approx 0.245
  • \Phi_1^{H} = \ln(0.245) \approx -1.406
  • \Phi_1^{\mathrm{sep}} = 2 \times (-1.406) = -2.812

Molecular H_2 (interleaved ordering):

The three transfer matrices are T_0 = T_{\mathfrak{p}_1 e_2}, T_1 = T_{e_2 \mathfrak{p}_2}^{\mathrm{dressed}}, T_2 = T_{\mathfrak{p}_2 e_1}. The covalent crossings (T_0 and T_2) have eigenvalues (q, -q^{-1}). The dressed intra-atomic crossing (T_1) has eigenvalues (q^5, -q^{-5}).

The traced volumes at each generator:

  \hat{V}_0 = z \cdot a_0 + b_0, \quad
  \hat{V}_1 = z \cdot a_1 + b_1, \quad
  \hat{V}_2 = z \cdot a_2 + b_2

where z = \mathrm{tr}_M(\mathcal{M}) / [3]_{q}! is the Markov-normalised trace variable.

The covalent channel (\sigma_1 mediating e_2--\mathfrak{p}_2) creates an additional attractive contribution that drives \Phi_1^{H_2} below \Phi_1^{\mathrm{sep}}. The binding energy from the LP dual:

  y_{\mathrm{cov}}^* = \Phi_1^{\mathrm{sep}} - \Phi_1^{H_2}
  = 2\Phi_1^H - \Phi_1^{H_2} > 0

The molecule binds when the shared-electron \Phi_1 reduction exceeds the proton-proton repulsion penalty.
rem:h2-bond-length-interpretation:
Remark H_2 bond length from covalent channel eigenvalue ratio. The covalent channel eigenvalue ratio \lambda_+/\lambda_- = q/q^{-1} = q^2 determines the effective bond length in the braid framework. The ratio q^2 \approx 1.231 measures how much the shared electron prefers one proton over the other:

  • q^2 = 1: perfectly symmetric sharing (equal eigenvalues), zero bond length (atoms coincide).
  • q^2 \to \infty: electron fully localised on one proton, no covalent bond.
  • q^2 \approx 1.231: moderate asymmetry, yielding an equilibrium distance where the attractive \Phi_1 reduction balances the repulsive proton-proton penalty.

The equilibrium bond length is set by the competition between:

  \frac{\partial \Phi_1^{\mathrm{attract}}}{\partial r}
  + \frac{\partial \Phi_1^{\mathrm{repel}}}{\partial r} = 0

where "distance" r in the braid framework is the number of intervening strands between the two protons. In H_4(q) with interleaved ordering [\mathfrak{p}_1, e_2, \mathfrak{p}_2, e_1], the protons are separated by one strand (one shared electron). The observed H_2 bond length is 0.74\;\text{\AA}.
sec:co-computation-intro: Carbon monoxide is the first heteronuclear test of the template. Carbon monoxide CO as a molecular braid joins the (6,6) carbon braid to the (8,8) oxygen braid with three shared electron pairs on a common strand set. The LP dual selects the triple bond as optimal for CO. Extract the CO triple bond energy from the Wedderburn invariants. Heteronuclear bonding requires no new machinery, only the asymmetric strand counts of the two atomic factors.
def:co-molecular-braid: Definition Carbon monoxide CO as a molecular braid. Carbon monoxide CO is the molecular braid of a carbon atom C(6, 6) and an oxygen atom O(8, 8) sharing three electron pairs (triple bond).
ex:co-molecular-braid-carbon-monoxide:
Example Building the carbon monoxide braid. The carbon monoxide braid is built explicitly in three stages.

Stage 1: Build the constituent atoms

Carbon: Z = 6, N = 6, A = 12. The atomic braid \mathcal{A}_C \in H_{18}(q) has 18 strands (12 nucleons + 6 electrons). Electron configuration 1s^2 2s^2 2p^2: four valence electrons in the n = 2 shell.

Oxygen: Z = 8, N = 8, A = 16. The atomic braid \mathcal{A}_O \in H_{24}(q) has 24 strands (16 nucleons + 8 electrons). Configuration 1s^2 2s^2 2p^4: two open valence sites, two lone pairs.

Stage 2: Molecular assembly in H_{42}(q)

The molecular braid lives in H_{42}(q) (18 + 24 = 42 strands). The triple bond involves 3 shared electron pairs (6 electrons total participating in covalent bonding):

  • 1 \sigma bond: one shared pair along the C--O axis
  • 2 \pi bonds: two shared pairs perpendicular to the axis

In the braid framework:

  • \sigma bond: one electron from C and one from O occupy adjacent strand positions, each with two \sigma^{-1} crossings (one to each nucleus)
  • \pi bonds: two additional shared pairs, each mediating between carbon's 2p shell and oxygen's 2p shell

After assembly:

  • Carbon retains: 2 core electrons (1s^2) + 1 lone pair = 4 non-bonding electrons
  • Oxygen retains: 2 core electrons (1s^2) + 1 lone pair = 4 non-bonding electrons
  • Shared: 6 electrons (3 pairs) in covalent channels

Stage 3: Iterative construction

The iterative constructor builds the molecular braid in steps:

  1. Start with \mathcal{A}_C (pre-computed, already in NF).
  2. Embed \mathcal{A}_O into the extended algebra.
  3. Apply inter-atomic nucleon crossings (all identity except \mathfrak{p}_C--\mathfrak{p}_O repulsion: 48 generator pairs).
  4. Apply covalent bond operators: 3 shared pairs \times 2 crossings each = 6 attractive \sigma^{-1} crossings.
  5. Gröbner--Shirshov reduce to normal form at each step.

The LP dual optimises the assignment of which 3 of carbon's 4 valence electrons are shared (and which 2 of oxygen's valence electrons are shared) by minimising \Phi_1 over all possible electron-bond assignments.
prop:co-lp-dual-binding: Proposition LP dual for CO: covalent active-set 2 (+ dative = triple). Conditional on Seven-term atomic mass formula with q-integer coefficients. For CO the covalent-bond-selection LP selects an active set of cardinality 2 — two orthogonal orbital channels \sigma \perp \pi, each an independent covalent channel rather than one accumulating chain of shared pairs. The observed triple bond is completed by a third, dative channel (an oxygen lone pair donated to carbon), giving total bond order 3 and making CO isoelectronic with \mathrm{N_2}.
rem:co-lp-dual-orthogonal-channels:
Remark Orthogonal-channel derivation of the CO bond order. This remark records the derivation behind LP dual for CO: covalent active-set 2 (+ dative = triple): why the multiple bond decomposes into orthogonal channels, why a single-chain model fails, and how the active-set cardinality reproduces the bond order.

Orthogonal channels, not one chain

A multiple bond is not one braid chain made "tighter" by stacking shared pairs into a common orbital. Each bond is an independent covalent channel — the reduced 4-strand [\mathfrak{p}_A,\, e_B,\, e_A,\, \mathfrak{p}_B] channel of H_2 — sitting in its own orthogonal orbital (\sigma head-on, \pi_x, \pi_y lateral). Because distinct orbitals are orthogonal, electrons in different channels share no e–e crossing. The channels bind independently and additively. The single \sigma channel binds at 0.8645\;\text{eV} (the H_2-scale covalent channel).

Failure of a single chain

Modelling the shared pairs as one interleaved (2k{+}2)-strand chain is computationally refuted. Only the first (\sigma) pair binds. The second and third pairs anti-bind because forcing every bonding electron into one orbital accumulates e–e repulsion — the braid-model expression of orbital exclusion. The bond-selection LP on that single-chain model has an active set of cardinality 1, not 3 (witness co-bond-order-active-set). The triple bond requires the orthogonal decomposition. A "decreasing-but-positive marginal in one chain" does not occur.

Bond order is occupied orthogonal channels

The bond-selection LP ranges over the orthogonal channels:

  \max_{x} \; \sum_{i \in \{\sigma,\, \pi_x,\, \pi_y\}} b_i\, x_i
  \quad\text{s.t.}\quad
  \sum_i x_i \le V_{CO}, \quad 0 \le x_i \le 1,

with each channel binding b_i > 0 and V_{CO} the shared valence budget. Its active set (the occupied orthogonal channels) has cardinality equal to the bond order. This is the molecular instance of the bond order = LP active-set cardinality identity.

For CO, the covalent budget is fixed by the octet valence of carbon and oxygen, derived ab initio below. An oxygen lone pair donated to carbon enters separately as a dative channel, not as a covalent LP term.

The orthogonal-channel LP \max_x \sum_i b_i x_i subject to \sum_i x_i \le \min(N_{\dim}, V) is computed for the diatomic series (witness co-bond-order-active-set), with the valence budget V derived ab initio from the octet rule (V_A = 10 - Z_A for second-row atoms: \mathrm{C}=4, \mathrm{N}=3, \mathrm{O}=2). The LP returns active-set cardinalities (\mathrm{O_2}, \mathrm{N_2}, \mathrm{CO}) = (2, 3, 2). For \mathrm{O_2} and \mathrm{N_2} this equals the observed bond order. For \mathrm{CO} the covalent active-set is 2. The observed triple bond includes one dative bond (an oxygen lone pair donated to carbon). This makes \mathrm{CO} isoelectronic with \mathrm{N_2}. The covalent count yields 2, and the dative channel is a named addition. The ceiling is N_{\dim} = 3: physical space \mathbb{R}^3 admits at most three mutually-orthogonal directions (one axial \sigma, two transverse \pi). No p-block bond exceeds order three. The active set is capped by the spatial dimension.

Two limitations remain. (i) The covalent valence derives from Z (octet rule), but \mathrm{CO}'s dative third bond is a named channel, not derived. (ii) The channels are modelled as equal independent copies, which overbinds the total energy (3\,b_\sigma versus the observed D_0) pending a lateral-\pi overlap reduction. The cardinality result holds; the energy is an upper bound.

The observed dissociation energy D_0(CO) \approx 11.09\;\text{eV} is consistent with three occupied channels. CO is isoelectronic with \mathrm{N_2}. Both carry three shared orthogonal channels with the same Hecke-algebra structure.
def:embeddable-knot-operator:
Definition Embeddable knot operator with geometric overlap weight. An embeddable knot operator is a knot operator K together with an embedding of its braid into the ambient 3-manifold, carrying an overlap weight w \in (0, 1] determined by the embedding direction relative to the bond axis. Its binding contribution is

  \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{bind}}(K) = \mathfrak{E}_0(K)\, w ,

where \mathfrak{E}_0(K) is the un-embedded channel binding. The operator is axial (\sigma-type) if its braid runs along the bond axis, in which case w = 1, and transverse (\pi-type) if its braid lies in the plane transverse to the bond axis, in which case w = w_\perp < 1, the transverse/axial overlap ratio fixed per system. The binding of a composite is the overlap-weighted sum

  \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{bind}}\Bigl(\textstyle\bigcup_i K_i\Bigr) = \sum_i \mathfrak{E}_0(K_i)\, w_i .
rem:embeddable-knot-operator-remark:
Remark Axial and transverse channels in an order-k bond. Head-on overlap is maximal for an axial (\sigma-type) channel, and lateral overlap is smaller for a transverse (\pi-type) channel; this is why w_\perp < 1.

An order-k bond is one axial \sigma channel and k-1 transverse \pi channels, with total binding \mathfrak{E}_0\,\bigl(1 + (k-1)\,w_\perp\bigr).
prop:bond-order-le-three: Proposition Bond order bounded by spatial dimension. Each bond channel embeds as a direction in the ambient 3-space, with distinct channels mutually orthogonal. Orthogonal nonzero vectors are linearly independent, so their number cannot exceed \dim_{\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{R}^3 = 3. At most three mutually-orthogonal channels embed — one axial \sigma and two transverse \pi. The bond order is bounded by the spatial dimension. No p-block bond exceeds order three.
rem:embeddable-cardinality-vs-energy: Remark Overlap weighting changes energy, not channel count. Overlap weighting changes only the energy, never the channel count. Every channel with w > 0 is occupied, so the active-set cardinality (the bond order of the CO LP dual) is independent of the weights. The equal-channel model (w \equiv 1) overbinds: for the \sigma + 2\pi triple bond it gives 1.42\times the observed D_0(\mathrm{N_2}). A lateral weight w_\perp \in [0.3, 0.7] brackets it (witness embeddable-knot-operator).
rem:co-triple-bond-energy:
Remark CO triple bond energy from the Wedderburn invariants. The CO bond energy decomposes into three Wedderburn channels:

  \mathfrak{E}_{\mathrm{bind}}(CO) = \alpha \sum_{i \in \mathrm{bonds}}
  \ln\lvert \hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{full}} \rvert

where the sum runs over all 6 covalent-channel generators (3 bonds \times 2 crossings each). The full traced volume includes symmetric, standard, and alternating representations:

  \hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{full}} =
  w_{\mathrm{sym}} \lambda_i^{\mathrm{sym}} +
  w_{\mathrm{std}} \hat{V}_i^{\mathrm{std}} +
  w_{\mathrm{alt}} \lambda_i^{\mathrm{alt}}

For the triple bond:

  • \sigma bond generators: eigenvalue products from the head-on overlap of 2s/2p_z orbitals.
  • \pi bond generators: eigenvalue products from lateral overlap of 2p_x and 2p_y orbitals.
  • The \sigma bond contributes the largest |\hat{V}| (strong overlap). The \pi bonds contribute smaller |\hat{V}| (weaker lateral overlap).

Scope. The bond energy below is not a parameter-free prediction. Its energy scale is fitted: the calibration factor 4.478/18.753 is the ratio that makes the uncalibrated result equal the measured \mathrm{H}_2 bond energy, a fourth calibration outside CAL-1/2/3. The three bonds are not differentiated in the recorded computation: each carries the identical \Delta\Phi_1 = 0.687012518457808, so the k=3 total is three times the k=1 value, contrary to the \sigma/\pi ordering stated above. No LP dual variables are recorded. The computed 13.434 eV is +21.1\% from D_0(\mathrm{CO}) = 11.09 eV, reached through a scale fitted on a different molecule, and is not cited here as derived.

The computation requires assembling the 42-strand transfer matrix chain. This is performed iteratively, reducing to NF at each step. The recorded computation contains:

  • \Phi_1 for isolated C and O atoms.
  • \Phi_1 for the CO molecular braid at each bond order k = 1, 2, 3.
  • The LP dual shadow prices y_1, y_2, y_3.
  • Comparison with observed D_0 \approx 11.09\;\text{eV}.
sec:co2-computation-intro: With heteronuclear bonding in place, add a third atom. Carbon dioxide CO_2 as a molecular braid couples a central carbon to two oxygens, each via a shared electron pair on the molecular Hecke strands. The LP dual selects linear O{=}C{=}O geometry. The optimum places the two C{=}O trefoils on opposite sides of the central strand. This configuration gives the VSEPR molecular geometry from \Phi_1 minimisation. The linear triatomic case isolates molecular geometry as a consequence of \Phi_1 minimisation, independent of bond order.
def:co2-molecular-braid: Definition Carbon dioxide CO_2 as a molecular braid. Carbon dioxide CO_2 is the molecular braid of one carbon atom C(6, 6) and two oxygen atoms O_1(8, 8), O_2(8, 8), with two double bonds (O=C=O), each consisting of one \sigma pair and one \pi pair.
